name: LM2574N-5.0_NOPB
title: LM2574, LM2574HV: 0.5 A step-down switching regulator, 40 V or 60 V input, fixed 3.3/5/12/15 V or adjustable
summary: A monolithic buck regulator with an internal 0.5 A power switch running at a fixed 52 kHz. The LM2574 takes up to 40 V in and the LM2574HV up to 60 V; each comes in 3.3 V, 5 V, 12 V and 15 V fixed versions and an adjustable version with a 1.23 V reference. Compensation is internal, and a complete supply needs four outside parts. An active-low ON/OFF input gives a 50 µA standby, and cycle-by-cycle current limit and thermal shutdown protect it. The LM2574N-5.0/NOPB is the 40 V, 5 V part in the 8-pin PDIP.
key_figures: 3.3, 5, 12, 15 V fixed; 1.23 V to 37 V (57 V HV) adjustable
4.75 V to 5.25 V over line, load and temperature

notes: LM2574 parts take up to 40 V in and LM2574HV parts up to 60 V. All are RoHS compliant and in production.

circuits.title: Fixed output voltage versions
circuits.description: The basic step-down converter for the 3.3, 5, 12 and 15 V parts. The internal switch chops the input onto OUTPUT; L1 and COUT average it into the output rail, and the Schottky D1 carries the inductor current while the switch is off. FB senses the output directly at COUT, ON/OFF is grounded so the part always runs, and CIN bypasses the input. Built with the LM2574HV, the same circuit takes up to 60 V in and supplies a 0.5 A load.

parts.note: Pulse 52627; for 5 V in and 3.3 V out, 100 µH RL-1284-100

notes: The leads from VIN to CIN and from OUTPUT to D1, and the ground returns of CIN, D1 and COUT, carry the high currents; they are kept as short as possible and meet at a single ground point.

circuits.title: Adjustable output voltage version, 5 V out
circuits.description: The adjustable part set to 5 V from a 7 to 60 V input. R2 (6.12 kΩ) and R1 (2 kΩ) divide the output down to the 1.23 V the feedback pin regulates to; the rest is the standard buck stage with L1, D1, COUT and the input capacitor CIN.

parts.value: 7 V to 60 V unregulated DC input

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for a buck circuit
circuits.description: Holds the regulator off until the input passes a threshold set by the zener. Below it Q1 is off and the 20 kΩ pull-up R3 takes ON/OFF high (off). Once VIN exceeds about VZ1 plus two base-emitter drops, current through R1 and Z1 turns Q1 on, which pulls ON/OFF low and lets the regulator run. The switch output, inductor, diode and feedback are those of the regulator's normal buck circuit.

circuits.title: Undervoltage lockout for a buck-boost circuit
circuits.description: The same zener-and-transistor lockout as for the buck circuit, adapted to the inverting converter: the emitter of Q1, the bottom of R2 and the regulator's ground pins all return to the negative output rail, while CIN stays on system ground. The rest of the converter is the inverting buck-boost circuit.

circuits.title: Delayed start-up
circuits.description: CD from VIN to ON/OFF and RD from ON/OFF to ground form an RC. At power-up CD couples the input step onto ON/OFF and holds the part off; as CD charges through RD the pin falls below the on threshold and switching begins. At 20 V in these values give about 10 ms of delay. The rest of the converter is the regulator's normal circuit.

circuits.title: 1.2-V to 55-V adjustable 500-mA supply with low output ripple
circuits.description: An LM2574HV-ADJ buck stage running from up to 60 V, with a 50 kΩ potentiometer R2 over a 1.1 kΩ R1 setting the output anywhere from 1.2 V to 55 V at 0.5 A. The potentiometer's wiper is tied to its lower end, so it acts as a variable resistor. An optional second LC stage, L2 (20 µH) and C1 (100 µF), after the main output capacitor cuts the output ripple and switching spikes by ten times or more. Feedback is taken before the filter.

parts.note: potentiometer, output voltage adjust; wiper joined to the R1 end

circuits.title: Inverting buck-boost, −12 V output
circuits.description: An LM2574-12 makes −12 V at up to about 100 mA from +8 to +25 V. The regulator's ground pins and ON/OFF ride on the negative output rail, and FB is tied to system ground, so the part regulates system ground to 12 V above its own ground; the output is therefore 12 V below ground. When the switch is on, L1 charges from the input; when it is off, L1 pushes current through D1 into COUT on the negative rail.

parts.value: +8 V to +25 V unregulated DC input

circuits.title: Negative boost, −5 V to −12 V in, −12 V out
circuits.description: An LM2574-12 steps a negative input of −5 V to −12 V up in magnitude to a regulated −12 V. VIN and FB are tied to system ground and the ground pins and ON/OFF sit on the −12 V output. L1 runs from the negative input to OUTPUT; the 1N5817 passes the inductor's energy into COUT. Load current is 60 mA at −5.2 V in and 120 mA at −7 V in.

operation.text: A non-synchronous step-down regulator with the power switch on chip, rated for 0.5 A of DC load. Inputs reach 40 V (LM2574) or 60 V (LM2574HV). Fixed parts give 3.3, 5, 12 or 15 V; the adjustable part covers 1.23 V to 37 V (57 V on the HV part) within ±4% over line and load. Compensation and a 52 kHz oscillator are internal; a working supply needs only an input capacitor, inductor, catch diode and output capacitor.

The feedback pin feeds a resistor divider into a fixed-gain error amplifier referred to a 1.23 V band-gap. A comparator against the 52 kHz oscillator drives the 0.5 A switch, whose collector is VIN and emitter OUTPUT. An internal regulator, thermal shutdown, current limit and an ON/OFF block complete it; signal and power grounds are separate pins.

The switch current is limited cycle by cycle; the peak limit is 0.7 to 1.6 A at 25 °C (1 A typical). If the output collapses by about 40% under a short or overload, the oscillator slows to roughly 18 kHz and the minimum duty cycle falls from 5% to about 2%, reducing the IC's average dissipation.
An on-chip thermal shutdown, together with the current limit, protects the part under fault conditions.

ON/OFF is active low. Above about 1.4 V the part is in standby, drawing 50 µA typical (200 µA maximum). Below about 1.2 V it switches and the output rises into regulation. For normal running the pin is grounded or driven by a TTL low (typically under 1.6 V); a TTL or CMOS high puts it in standby. The pin may be tied directly to +VIN with no series resistor, and it must never be left open.
A zener, an NPN and three resistors on ON/OFF keep the part off until the input reaches about VZ1 + 2 VBE, for the buck or the buck-boost form.

An RC from VIN onto ON/OFF holds the part off at power-up; 0.1 µF and 47 kΩ give roughly 10 ms at 20 V in. A larger time constant gives more delay, but with a lot of 60 Hz or 120 Hz ripple on the input it couples that ripple onto ON/OFF and can cause trouble.

VIN needs at least 22 µF of electrolytic bypass, on short leads close to the regulator, for stability. Below about −25 °C more may be needed, since electrolytic capacitance falls and ESR rises with cold and with age; a ceramic or solid tantalum in parallel improves stability in the cold. For long capacitor life its RMS ripple current rating must exceed 1.2 × (tON/T) × ILOAD.

The part works with the inductor current either always flowing (continuous) or falling to zero for part of each cycle (discontinuous). Continuous running gives better load regulation, lower peak currents in switch, inductor and diode, and can give lower output ripple, at the cost of larger inductance at light load. Any buck converter goes discontinuous at light enough load, and that is acceptable. The inductor guides assume continuous conduction and let the allowed ripple, as a share of load current, grow as the design load falls, which keeps the inductor small.

For 5 V at 0.4 A from 10 to 20 V, the 5-V guide points to 330 µH. Near the top of that region (20 V in) the ripple is 53% of 0.4 A, 212 mA peak to peak. That gives a 506 mA peak inductor and switch current and a 106 mA load below which operation turns discontinuous; ripple times the output capacitor's ESR gives the output ripple. If the guide's value is impractically large, discontinuous operation is worth considering.

Bobbin-core inductors on an open ferrite rod are cheapest but leak flux, which raises EMI and can induce false readings in a scope probe. An inductor driven past its rated current saturates: its inductance collapses, current climbs quickly toward the winding resistance limit, and the inductor can overheat. The listed Pulse Engineering parts are powdered-iron toroids and the Renco parts ferrite bobbins.

COUT filters the output and sets loop stability, and must sit close to the regulator on short traces. Ordinary aluminium electrolytics usually work; low-ESR types give lower ripple and better stability. ESR depends on value, voltage rating, size and construction, and small or low-voltage (under 12 V) electrolytics tend to be higher. 100 µF to 330 µF typically leave 50 mV to 150 mV of ripple, larger values about 20 mV to 50 mV, and paralleled or low-ESR grades 10 mV to 20 mV. In continuous mode an ESR below 0.03 Ω can make the loop unstable, so a tantalum alone needs care; tantalum making up 10% to 20% of the total alongside aluminium helps at low temperature. The capacitor's ripple current rating at 52 kHz must be at least 1.5 times the inductor's ripple current (peak to peak).

Standard aluminium electrolytics of 100 µF to 1000 µF have roughly 0.5 Ω to 0.1 Ω ESR; premium (low-ESR) grades in that range are generally below 0.15 Ω. ESR heats the capacitor and shortens its life, and in the output filter it sets the ripple; ESL causes spikes on the output of a buck converter.

The diode returns inductor current while the switch is off and must sit close to the regulator on short leads and traces. Schottky diodes give the best efficiency, especially below 5 V out. Fast-recovery, high-efficiency and ultra-fast diodes also work, but those with an abrupt turn-off can cause instability and EMI; soft recovery is better. 60 Hz rectifiers such as the 1N4001 or 1N5400 are not suitable.

The output carries a sawtooth ripple at the switching frequency, typically about 1% of VOUT, mostly inductor ripple current times COUT's ESR, plus short spikes at the sawtooth peaks from fast switching and the capacitor's parasitic inductance. Low-inductance capacitors on short leads reduce the spikes; wiring inductance, stray capacitance and the scope probe all add to their measured size. A second LC stage of 20 µH and 100 µF can cut ripple and spikes tenfold.

On fixed versions FB is wired to the output voltage point. On the adjustable version both programming resistors go close to the regulator, to keep noise off the feedback node, and values above 100 kΩ are avoided for the same reason. R1 is 1 k to 5 k; 1% metal-film resistors give the best temperature coefficient and long-term stability.

With the ground pins on the negative output and FB grounded, a −12 V part regulates its output to −12 V. From 8 V in or more it supplies about 100 mA; with less load it keeps working down to about 4.7 V in. Switch currents run higher than in a buck, and start-up input current can overload a source limited below 0.6 A; delayed start-up or undervoltage lockout lets the input rise first. The buck design guides do not apply: use 68 µH to 220 µH, and a larger output capacitor than a buck needs, into the thousands of µF at low input or high load. The regulator sees the sum of input and output magnitudes, so for −12 V out the input limit is 28 V (LM2574) or 48 V (LM2574HV).

Takes −5 V to −12 V in and gives a regulated −12 V. An input more negative than −12 V pushes the output past −12 V without harming the regulator. Switch current is high, particularly at low input, and the switch rating limits load current. A boost cannot limit current into a shorted load, so another protection such as a fuse may be needed.

Example: 5 V out, 15 V maximum in, 0.4 A load. On the guide for the output voltage, the 15 V and 0.4 A lines meet in the 330 µH region; pick an inductor from the manufacturer table (PE-52627, RL-1284-330 or NP5920/5921), rated for 52 kHz and 1.5 × ILOAD. COUT of 100 µF to 470 µF aluminium electrolytic sets the dominant pole pair with L and gives about 1% ripple; rate it at least 1.5 × VOUT (8 V minimum, 10 V or 15 V suggested for 5 V; 20 V chosen), as higher-voltage parts often have lower ESR. The catch diode is rated for 1.5 × the maximum load, or for the full current limit if the output must survive a continuous short; 1 A is enough for this example, with reverse voltage at least 1.25 × VIN(max): a 20 V 1N5817 or SR102. CIN is 22 µF aluminium close to the input and ground pins.

Example: 24 V out, 40 V maximum in, 0.4 A, 52 kHz. R1 = 1 k and R2 = 18.7 k set the output. E × T works out to 185 V × µs; on the adjustable guide with 0.4 A this falls in the 1000 µH region, and the inductor is chosen from the table, rated for 52 kHz and 1.5 × ILOAD. The stability rule asks for COUT above 22.2 µF, but acceptable ripple calls for 100 µF, rated at least 35 V. The stability formula gives values between 5 µF and 1000 µF; ripple and transient response may need several times more. The diode is a 50 V MBR150 or 11DQ05 at 1 A.

Switching waveforms are characterised at 5 V out in continuous conduction (500 mA, L = 330 µH) and in discontinuous conduction (100 mA, L = 100 µH). Load-step response is characterised from 100 mA to 500 mA (L = 330 µH, COUT = 300 µF) and from 50 mA to 250 mA (L = 68 µH, COUT = 470 µF).

Fast-changing currents in wiring inductance make voltage spikes, so the high-current leads are kept as short as possible and grounds meet at a single point or on a plane. The key rule is small AC current loops: the loop through the input capacitor, switch and catch diode carries the abruptly changing current and its traces are kept short and wide. Place the regulator, bypass capacitor, Schottky diode, inductor and the feedback resistors (R1 = RFBB, R2 = RFBT) compactly, with the programming resistors near the regulator. A copper weight of 2 oz or more helps heat spreading and lowers trace inductance. The ground plane area also matters for dissipation.
Power ground and signal ground are separate pins on both packages; each is soldered directly to wide copper for low inductance and good heat flow.

Both packages have solid copper lead frames that carry most of the die heat through the leads into the board, whose copper does the heat sinking. Wide traces and soldering all ground and unused pins to large copper areas lower the thermal resistance; double-sided and multilayer boards help further. A socket for the 8-pin part adds thermal resistance and is advised against unless power is small. Dissipation ranges from about 0.1 W to 0.75 W, and on a well-laid-out board either package handles 0.75 W at 60 °C ambient with the junction below 125 °C. Board size, copper area and thickness, nearby heat sources such as the diode and inductor, and airflow all change the real figure; the junction temperature can be found by measuring copper temperature next to the IC with a small thermocouple and adding θj-cu × PD.
The built-in ESD protection is limited; keep the leads shorted together or the part in conductive foam during storage and handling.
